« Ça fait mal » : le discours sur l’immi: “It hurts”: the discourse on immigration and housing is troubling
Elle-même mère monoparentale et sans sta: A single mother without status herself, she struggles to understand the prevailing discourse.
Depuis quelques semaines, des politicien: For several weeks now, politicians and economists have been warning the public about immigration, which is said to be partly responsible for the “housing crisis.” At the heart of the discussions, numbers are being invoked – absorption capacity, a question of math – but asylum seekers and people who work in immigration see a risk in this.
La Converse les a appelés à réagir aux p: La Converse asked them to react to the possible effects of the prevailing discourse.
Nina Gonzales* a la voix qui tremble un: Nina Gonzales* has a slight tremor in her voice. The subject currently making headlines fills her with a certain indignation.
« Les politiciens sont capables de parle: “Politicians are able to speak and say harsh, cruel words against immigrants. People forget that we fled our countries of origin [...] and that if we're talking about temporary workers, we come here to try to improve our quality of life, for ourselves and our families,” says this activist for the rights of workers without status, over the phone. “It hurts!”
Rappelons, entre autres déclarations, qu: Among other statements, it's worth recalling that Conservative Party of Canada leader <l1>Pierre Poilievre has repeatedly said that the intake of immigrants must be tied to the construction of housing.</l1>
Au-delà de la question du logement, le p: Beyond the housing question, the burden of immigration, particularly irregular immigration, on social services has also been raised. All this follows the publication of a National Bank study on absorption capacity, which estimates that Canada is rushing into a “demographic trap.”
Puis, le 18 janvier 2024, le premier min: Then, on January 18, 2024, Quebec Premier François Legault sent a letter to Ottawa asking for help in the face of the “influx of asylum seekers” that risks bringing the Belle Province to a “breaking point.”
Depuis, le ministre de l’Immigration du: Since then, Canada's immigration minister has announced new assistance for the provinces for <l1>the reception of asylum seekers, totalling $362 million.</l1>
Du côté de la Table de concertation des: At the Table de concertation des organismes au service des personnes réfugiées et immigrantes (TCRI), there was no question of staying silent. The coalition of more than 155 organizations working with asylum seekers and refugees denounced the use of these people as scapegoats “to explain the crisis in public services,” and said that “announcing a ‘breaking point’ amounts to ignoring the multiple roots of this crisis,” in a press release published the day after Quebec's letter to the federal government was sent.
« Présenter l’arrivée des demandeurs d’a: “Presenting the arrival of asylum seekers as a crisis for the Quebec state sweeps under the rug the fact that these people are themselves in crisis and are fleeing situations of persecution and violence in many forms,” says Louis-Philippe Jannard, coordinator of the TCRI's Protection division, in an email sent to La Converse.
« D’entrée de jeu, il ne s’agit pas de n: “Right off the bat, this isn't about denying the housing crisis. It's a real issue that causes hardship for a great many people, including newcomers, in all immigration categories.”
« Ce n’est pas du tout avec un débat par: “A debate like this is not at all how we're going to solve any public policy problem whatsoever. I find that the fact that this debate is skewed this way, and that it can be interpreted as targeting particular communities, has nothing but negative effects,” says Adèle Garnier, professor in the Department of Geography at Université Laval. “I absolutely do not see the positive side of this debate. It is positive to talk about immigration in the public arena and to want to discuss the situation and the importance of temporary migration.”
La chercheuse de l’Équipe de recherche s: The researcher with the Équipe de recherche sur l'immigration au Québec et ailleurs (ERIQA) laments governments' inaction in the face of calls from experts in the field who say that planning around immigration needs to be addressed. The current discourse simply leads to “stigmatizing these [immigrant or asylum-seeking] communities even more. It endangers social cohesion and does absolutely nothing to solve the problems of the housing crisis,” she says.
Une crainte partagée par plusieurs de no: A fear shared by several of the people we spoke to, including Nina Gonzales.
Des chiffres qui ne disent pas tout: Numbers that don't tell the whole story
La chercheuse et professeure en sociolog: For her part, Carole Yerochewski, a retired researcher and sociology professor at Université de Montréal, recalls a statement made about immigrants by former Quebec immigration minister Jean Boulet. During the 2022 election campaign, he let slip during a radio debate that “80% of immigrants go to Montréal, don't work, don't speak French or don't adhere to the values of Quebec society.”
Dès lors, mentionne Mme Yerochewski, « o: From that point on, says Ms. Yerochewski, “you can speak like that in the public square; you can start to revive discourse that is, in fact, xenophobic.”
« [Les immigrants], on vient ici pour am: “[Immigrants], we come here to improve our lives and those of our children. It's appalling and it's unacceptable that people say that so easily in public,” adds Nina Gonzales.
Après le déliement de la parole, poursui: After the loosening of tongues, Ms. Yerochewski continues, “the second step is that economists show up with numbers that support these little soundbites. The problem is that you'll always find economists to back up what you're saying and others to go against [your idea], because economics is not an exact science.”
La troisième étape, toujours selon la so: The third step, according to the sociologist, is the appearance of measures.
« On pouvait le dire depuis des décennie: “We could have said for decades that the housing crisis was coming, but the current staging is very forceful.”
D’ailleurs, au vu de la confusion dans l: Moreover, given the confusion among migration statuses – permanent residents, temporary workers, asylum seekers, international students – it is hard to say who this discourse is attacking.

This means they live in a dwelling with fewer bedrooms than their household size requires. A figure far from the 9% for the general population.

« Ceux qui ne rentrent pas par la grande: “Those who don't come in through the front door now outnumber those who come in through regular channels. The question of immigration thresholds, which is mostly tied to the concept of the regular immigrant, is brushed aside.”
Celui qui a aussi travaillé en intégrati: Ryan, who has also worked on newcomer integration, explains that this shortcut is very appealing to politicians because it allows them to “sidestep the real sources of the problem.”
Jointe à son bureau de Québec, Adèle Gar: Reached at her office in Quebec City, Adèle Garnier laments that a “very complex” issue is being simplified in this way. “There's a kind of focus, a spotlight on the numbers. And that's really [present, for example, with] the question of thresholds – with numbers. To me, that's still quite new in the Canadian debate,” she says. This strategy of numbers allows politicians “to avoid engaging in xenophobia,” because they don't blame a particular community, but rather “categories.”
« On dit, par exemple, que les migrants: “For example, they say there are too many temporary migrants,” continues the professor in Université Laval's Department of Geography. “I still think it's dangerous [because of] the impact on public debate, because it's clear [...] that there will be individual impacts and that some communities will feel more targeted than others.”

Si le manque de logements semble être un: While the lack of housing seems to be a factor cited in political discourse to explain the “housing crisis,” this reading ignores affordability issues, according to some of the people consulted by La Converse.

Tomorrow morning, you can say all you want, ‘We're going to take in fewer immigrants,’ but where are you really going to cut?”
L’Institut de recherche et d’information: The Institut de recherche et d'informations socioéconomiques (IRIS) also notes that average rent rose 3.6% in Quebec from October 2021 to October 2022 when the tenant stayed the same, but 13% when the tenant changed.
« Cette différence met en évidence le fa: “This difference highlights the fact that rental housing owners are taking advantage of the end of a lease to raise the rent to a level exceeding the increases recommended by the Tribunal administratif du logement,” <l1>reads the IRIS report.</l1>

« C’est un gouvernement qui n’est pas ca: “It's a government that's not capable of building social housing; it's not the immigrants' fault, it's the governments' fault, it's a crisis that's been here for a long time. Régularisation des personnes sans statut: Regularizing people without status: fear of a reversal
En décembre 2021, le premier ministre ca: In December 2021, Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau asked the then immigration minister to propose a way to regularize the situation of people without status. Pressed by grassroots organizations such as the Migrant Rights Network, Minister Marc Miller finally announced in December 2023 that a “broad program” to regularize undocumented people would be coming. People without status are estimated to number 500,000 in Canada (it is impossible to confirm these figures).
Une question, cependant, se pose : le di: One question arises, however: will the current discourse make the minister back down? That is what some of the people we consulted fear.
« Le problème, c’est qu’on voit s’éloign: “The problem is that we see the prospect of a regularization program receding and, it must be pointed out, it doesn't make the cause of regularization sympathetic, whereas it very much was coming out of the pandemic,” says Ms. Yerochewski. “We knew it was undocumented people and asylum seekers who had kept working, kept exposing themselves. This discourse no longer makes them sympathetic…”
Qualifiant le discours actuel faisant l’: Calling the current discourse that conflates the housing crisis and immigration quite “violent,” Ms. Garnier is not surprised. “This discourse is part of a dynamic of polarization around immigration in Quebec [that we've observed] pretty much since 2018.” A polarization that opens the door to a change of course, even within public opinion.
La professeure Garnier cite un sondage d: Professor Garnier cites an October poll produced by the firm Environics. “Canadians are now markedly more likely than a year ago to say there is too much immigration to the country” – a reversal of a trend observed for 30 years. “For the first time, a growing number of Canadians are questioning the number of immigrants arriving in the country, rather than their identity and origin,”<l1> the researchers note</l1>.
Devant ce durcissement de l’opinion publ: In the face of this hardening of public opinion on immigration, compounded by some recent announcements (think of the measures that will affect international students, notably the 35% reduction in study permits issued by the federal government), the promise of regularization appears weakened.
« Mais pendant la pandémie, c’étaient le: “But during the pandemic, it was the immigrants, the temporary workers, it was us who were there,” Nina recalls. “We think we can sort out our situation in Canada, [...] but in the end it's hard for people without status or immigrants to live as if we were criminals.
